sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The arrival of Europeans in what is now Botswana marked a profound turning point in the region's history. It was not a single event but a gradual process spanning nearly a century, beginning with isolated travellers and hunters in the late 18th century and culminating in the establishment of the Bechuanaland Protectorate in 1885. The European presence brought new technologies, new religions, new economic systems, and ultimately, colonial rule. However, the Tswana were not passive recipients of these changes; they actively engaged with, resisted, and adapted to European influences, shaping their own destiny in the process.

Bechuanaland was first visited by Europeans towards the close of the **18th century**. The generally peaceful disposition of the tribes rendered the opening up of the country comparatively easy. When European traders and missionaries began arriving in Botswana in the **early nineteenth century**, they found the lives of most Botswana communities being disrupted by Bakololo and Amandebele invaders. As a result, a number of more powerful rulers emerged—such as **Sebego of the Bangwaketse**, **Sechele of the Bakwena**, **Sekgoma of the Bangwato**, and **Letsholathebe of the Batawana**—who built up their emerging states by acquiring both knowledge and guns from the European visitors.

subsections.title: The Hunters' Paradise
subsections.content:
Before the railway arrived towards the end of the 19th century, the Tati District—a semi-arid triangular-shaped area between the Shashi and Ramokgwebane Rivers in Bechuanaland (now Botswana)—was described as **"Africa at its wildest and most untamed – a hunters' paradise"**. It was this initially, and in later years the discovery of gold, that caused the white man to ignore the threat of fever, dysentery and other dangers and venture into this unexplored region.

European hunters, miners, explorers and missionaries were active in the Tati district from the **1850s to the end of the 1890s**. These early visitors were drawn by the abundant wildlife, particularly elephants, whose ivory was highly prized in European markets. The hunting trade had significant ecological impacts, decimating elephant populations and other large game. In return for guns, the Tswana chiefs traded ivory and other game products.

subsections.title: The Ox Wagon Age
subsections.content: The ox wagon age in Botswana began fairly slowly with the intrusion into it by the first European travellers, traders, hunters and missionaries in the first part of the 19th century. Because of the economic circumstances of the country, it would have lasted longer than in more developed regions. The ox wagon became the primary means of transport for Europeans penetrating the interior, and its arrival symbolised the beginning of a new era of mobility and connection to the wider world.

subsections.title: The Pioneers of Christian Evangelism
subsections.content:
The **London Missionary Society (LMS)** was the most significant missionary organisation in Botswana. Its arrival in the early 1800s started the most notable work of missionaries in Botswana. The LMS missionaries were the best known of all the Christian missionaries in Southern Africa, especially in present-day Botswana. To a large extent, the LMS missionaries can be presented as having been at the forefront of pioneering missionary outreach throughout much of the area beyond the borders of the Cape Colony during the nineteenth century.

The missionaries who were the most prominent members of the LMS were **Robert Moffat**, **David Livingstone**, **John Mackenzie**, and **William Charles Willoughby**.

subsections.title: The Establishment of Mission Stations
subsections.content:
The London Missionary Society established stations in what is now Griqualand West in 1803. In **1818**, the mission station of **Kuruman** (near present-day Vryburg in South Africa), in Bechuanaland proper, was founded. Although Kuruman is now in South Africa, it served as the primary base for missionary activity throughout the Bechuanaland region.

From Kuruman, Christianity very gradually spread to the interior. Missionaries settled amongst the people, often **at the invitation of the chiefs** who wanted guns and knew that the presence of missionaries encouraged the traders. By **1880**, every major village of every tribe in Botswana had a resident missionary, and their influence had become a permanent feature of life.

subsections.title: Missionary Methods
subsections.content:
The missionaries worked through the chief, recognising that **the chief's conversion was the key to the rest of the tribe**. Chiefs' responses varied widely—from Khama's (of the Bangwato) wholehearted embrace of the faith, to Sekgoma Letsholathebe's (of the Batawana) outright rejection, which he claimed was in defence of his culture.

The missionaries made the mistake of believing that to become a Christian, Batswana had to completely abandon their indigenous cultures. They treated African religions as evil and did everything possible to ensure that it was ousted. The western missionaries believed that traditional religious beliefs and practices were inferior, and together with the traditional customs, had to be done away with before the acceptance of Christianity. However, this was vehemently resisted.

subsections.title: Robert Moffat (1795–1883)
subsections.content:
Robert Moffat was a **Scottish missionary and linguist** who worked in South Africa and Botswana for more than **60 years**. He arrived in South Africa in 1817 under the aegis of the London Missionary Society. He pioneered missionary activity among the Tswana people and became deeply influential in Southern Africa, helping to open up the interior.

Moffat's most enduring achievement was **reducing the Bechuana tongue to writing**—developing a written form of the Setswana language. He also translated the Bible into Setswana, laying the foundation for literacy and education in the region. Largely as the result of his work, and of other missionaries, the Bechuana advanced notably in civilisation.

Moffat's influence extended beyond his own work: his daughter, **Mary Moffat**, married **David Livingstone**, creating a dynastic connection between two of the most significant figures in the history of southern African missions.

subsections.title: David Livingstone (1813–1873)
subsections.content:
**David Livingstone** was a Scottish missionary and explorer who first came to South Africa in **1841** to found a mission station among the Kwena of SECHELE. His arrival in **1841** marked the beginning of the systematic exploration of the northern regions.

Livingstone worked out of Kuruman for about two years, and then married Moffat's daughter, Mary. Though much more interested in exploration than missionary work, and later much more involved in the abolition of the slave trade, Livingstone set up a mission station at **Kolobeng** among the Bakwena.

Tired of working in one place, in the late 1840s he explored **northern Botswana** in search of new mission fields. In **1851** he reached the **Zambezi River**, where he met the Kololo king SEBITWANE. Livingstone was enthused by the idea of opening a mission among the Kololo; he set as his life's work expanding Christian frontiers in Africa.

Livingstone's travels covered almost every part of the country hitherto unknown. Along the way, he saw and named the **Victoria Falls**. His travels, and those of C.I.Anderson (1853–1858) and others, opened up the interior to European knowledge.

Livingstone's somewhat exaggerated descriptions of the slave trade encouraged European intervention and eventual occupation of Eastern Africa. His reputation in Europe was boosted tremendously by **Henry Stanley**, who visited him at Lake Tanganyika (1871) and then returned home to portray him as a martyr in the cause of African redemption.

subsections.title: John Mackenzie (1835–1899)
subsections.content:
**John Mackenzie** was a British missionary who was a **constant champion of the rights of Africans** in Southern Africa and a proponent of British intervention to curtail the spread of Boer influence, especially over the lands of the Tswana peoples.

A member of the London Missionary Society, Mackenzie went to Southern Africa in **1858** and began his missionary work at Kuruman and continued in the Tswana territories known as Bechuanaland. He lived at **Shoshong** in present-day Botswana from **1862 to 1876**.

Troubled by the growing encroachments on Tswana territories by Boers from the Transvaal republic to the east, he was active from **1867** in attempts to have Britain declare a protectorate over Tswana territories, claiming that the British would safeguard African rights from Boer racism.

In **1884**, a protectorate was declared over the southern Tswana territories, known as **British Bechuanaland** (now in northern South Africa), with Mackenzie as its deputy commissioner. He lost this job to **Cecil Rhodes** in 1885 but remained in politics, retaining a great deal of influence. Later that year, he participated in the **Warren Expedition**, which resulted in the Tswana lands north of British Bechuanaland being declared the **Bechuanaland Protectorate** (now Botswana).

subsections.title: The Rev. John Campbell
subsections.content: The Rev. John Campbell, one of the founders of the Bible Society, also travelled in southern Bechuanaland and the adjoining districts in **1812–1814** and **1819–1821**, adding considerably to the knowledge of the river systems.

subsections.title: Gustav Fritsch (1838–1927)
subsections.content:
The **German explorer** Gustav Fritsch arrived in **1865** at the community of **Moshupa**, in what is today southeastern Botswana. There he saw a large crowd of people singing Christian hymns and listening to African preachers.

Fritsch was a German anatomist, anthropologist, traveller and physiologist. From **1863–66**, he travelled from Cape Town through the Orange Free State, Basutoland, Natal, and Bechuanaland. He was a 25-year-old medical doctor and anthropologist who travelled through southern Africa on a scientific expedition to study the 'native races', making great use of the new medium of photography.

In his observations, he expressed views which would become the dominant view of African-European relations during the colonial era and beyond. Missing from Fritsch's descriptions was an awareness of African perspectives during the decades prior to European conquest, such as those of the 'native preacher' who led the worship service in Moshupa and therefore was the primary local agent of modernisation.

subsections.title: Alfred Wookey (1847–1917)
subsections.content:
**Alfred Wookey** was a missionary of the London Missionary Society who led a mission establishment in the **Khwebe Hills** of Ngamiland during the **1890s**. He tried to create a utopian settlement in the Khwebe Hills, far from what he perceived as the corrupting dangers of the Batawana town, or the threat to health of Lake Ngami.

Wookey also wrote a history of the Bechuana in Setswana: **"Dinwao leha e le dipolelo kaga dicò tsa secwana"** (History of the Bechuana). His work is a valuable historical record of Tswana traditions and history.

sections.title: African Agency and Resistance
sections.content: The arrival of Europeans was not a one-way process of imposition. African evangelists played a crucial role in the spread of Christianity. The leading African preacher in Moshupa and nearby communities during the 1860s was **Paulo Rrafifing Molefane**. As well as being one of the early African evangelists, as ambassador, cultural broker, and purveyor of foreign goods and ideas, Paulo also became involved in the tensions that accompanied a growing European presence during the mid-nineteenth century. The ties which he and his family formed between Europeans and Africans played an important role in the development of early African-European relations. The figure of Paulo Rrafifing Molefane demonstrates the significant levels of contestation, cultural malleability, and individual initiative that arose in the broad, indeterminate borderland between African and European.

subsections.title: The Batswana's Pre-Existing Religious Traditions
subsections.content:
Historical evidence shows that Batswana possessed **rich cultural and religious traditions** that contributed to the rapid spread of Christianity in Bechuanaland Protectorate. The underlying patterns of these cultural and religious traditions and systems of the Batswana provided a firm foundation upon which Christianity was conceived, understood and received.

The Batswana had an **absolute belief in a Supreme Being**, whom they referred to as **Modimo**. This pre-existing concept of a Supreme Being made the Christian message more comprehensible and acceptable to many Tswana people. Some missionaries gave the impression that no such religious traditions and heritage existed prior to their arrival on the African continent, but this was a misconception.

subsections.title: Chiefs' Strategic Engagement
subsections.content:
The Tswana chiefs were not passive recipients of European influence. They actively **invited missionaries** to establish schools in their territories because they recognised the strategic value of European knowledge and technology. In return for guns, they traded ivory and other game products.

The missionaries worked through the chief, recognising that **the chief's conversion was the key to the rest of the tribe**. This gave the chiefs considerable leverage. Chiefs' responses varied widely—from **Khama's** (of the Bangwato) wholehearted embrace of the faith, to **Sekgoma Letsholathebe's** (of the Batawana) outright rejection, which he claimed was in defence of his culture.

subsections.title: Resistance to Cultural Imposition
subsections.content: The Batswana challenged and rejected the western superiority complex that the missionaries adopted as unacceptable and undermining their integrity. Through misconceptions that saw education, commerce and trade as integral to their work, the missionaries tried to impose their Western cultural values on the Batswana. However, this was vehemently resisted.

subsections.title: Education and Literacy
subsections.content:
The London Missionary Society came to Botswana in the 19th Century and was the **first group of people to provide formal education**. The first school was established by David Livingstone among Bakgatla ba ga Mmanaana in the **1840s**.

The missionaries developed written forms of Tswana languages, translated the Bible, and established printing presses and schools. It was LMS missionaries, most notably the Rev. Robert Moffat, who pioneered the development of the first Setswana publications, as well as schools through printing press and college at Kudumane.

subsections.title: The Transformation of Tswana Identity
subsections.content: European missionaries played an **important role in the evolution of the term 'Batswana'** and the adoption of that meaning by both Europeans and Batswana. Through their long years of residence among Tswana people and their development of written forms of Tswana languages, missionaries became acknowledged by other Europeans as **experts on Tswana culture**. Their notions of Tswana ethnicity became incorporated into European understandings of Africans and, eventually, into Tswana understandings of themselves.

subsections.title: Guns and Political Power
subsections.content: The arrival of Europeans brought **firearms**, which fundamentally altered the balance of power among the Tswana kingdoms. Chiefs who had access to guns could defend their territories against Ndebele raiders and Boer encroachment, and could also assert dominance over rival Tswana groups. In return for guns, they traded ivory and other game products.

subsections.title: The Boer Threat
subsections.content: The **Transvaal Boers invaded Botswana in 1852**, but were driven away by a coalition of merafe (tribes) who temporarily united under the overall leadership of the Bakwena ruler **Sechele**. This invasion highlighted the growing threat from European settlers and the need for Tswana unity.

subsections.title: The Path to the Protectorate
subsections.content: The arrival of Europeans ultimately led to the establishment of the **Bechuanaland Protectorate in 1885**. The Tswana chiefs, led by Khama III of the Bangwato, Gaseitsiwe of the Bangwaketse, and others, petitioned the British government for protection against Boer annexation. The British, concerned about German expansion in South-West Africa and Boer ambitions, agreed to establish a protectorate—but significantly, not a colony. The Tswana chiefs retained their authority over internal affairs, while Britain controlled foreign policy and provided military protection.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The arrival of Europeans in Botswana was a complex and transformative process. It brought new technologies, new religions, new economic systems, and ultimately, colonial rule. However, the Tswana were not passive victims of this process. They actively engaged with, resisted, and adapted to European influences. Chiefs strategically invited missionaries to gain access to guns and knowledge. African evangelists like Paulo Rrafifing Molefane played crucial roles in spreading Christianity on their own terms. The pre-existing Tswana belief in a Supreme Being (Modimo) provided a foundation for understanding Christianity.

The European arrival set in motion changes that would culminate in the establishment of the Bechuanaland Protectorate, the preservation of Tswana political structures, and eventually, the peaceful transition to independence in 1966. The story of European arrival in Botswana is not simply a story of European imposition, but of African agency, adaptation, and resilience.

keyFigures.name: Robert Moffat
keyFigures.description: Scottish missionary and linguist who worked in South Africa and Botswana for more than 60 years. He reduced the Bechuana tongue to writing and translated the Bible into Setswana. His daughter married David Livingstone.

keyFigures.name: David Livingstone
keyFigures.description: Scottish missionary and explorer who came to South Africa in 1841. Founded a mission at Kolobeng among the Bakwena. Explored northern Botswana, reached the Zambezi in 1851, and named Victoria Falls. His travels opened up the interior to European knowledge.

keyFigures.name: John Mackenzie
keyFigures.description: British missionary and champion of African rights. Lived at Shoshong (1862–1876). Advocated for British protectorate over Tswana territories to counter Boer influence. Served as deputy commissioner of British Bechuanaland and participated in the Warren Expedition that established the Bechuanaland Protectorate.

keyFigures.name: John Campbell
keyFigures.description: One of the founders of the Bible Society. Travelled in southern Bechuanaland in 1812–1814 and 1819–1821, adding to knowledge of river systems.

keyFigures.name: Gustav Fritsch
keyFigures.description: German explorer, anatomist, and anthropologist. Travelled through southern Africa (1863–66) on a scientific expedition. Observed Christian worship at Moshupa in 1865. His views became dominant in colonial-era African-European relations.

keyFigures.name: Alfred Wookey
keyFigures.description: LMS missionary who led a mission in the Khwebe Hills of Ngamiland in the 1890s. Wrote a history of the Bechuana in Setswana: 'Dinwao leha e le dipolelo kaga dicò tsa secwana' (History of the Bechuana).
